subject: Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log

messages.author: 129e07bdb789652f
messages.subject: Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
Hello, 

 I was a WinBUGS user a couple of years ago, and now I'm back in Bayesian statistics. I'm a newbie in Stan.

In order to train myself, I have programmed the model in Tunaru's paper "Hierarchical Bayesian Models for Multiple Count Data".  There's a slight difference in my model as compared to the original model given in the paper: I add a known parameter S_{k,i} in the mean of the Poisson distributions (S_{k,i}=1 in the paper and in my code the indices are S_{i,j}). This is not important. 

Firstly I simulate some data and I fit the model with JAGS: 

###########################
### simulations of data ###
###########################
library(mvtnorm)
set.seed(666)
N <- 50
M <- 3
Sigma0 <- rWishart(1, df=M+1, diag(M))[,,1]/5
S <- matrix(100, nrow=N, ncol=M)
Mu <- rep(0,M)
Lambda <-  exp(rmvnorm(N, Mu, Sigma0))
Y <- matrix(rpois(N*M, Lambda*S), nrow=N)
colnames(Y) <- paste0("y", 1:M)

###########################
###     JAGS model      ###
###########################
library(rjags)
# write the model #
model.file <- "Tunaru.jags" 
wb.model <- function(){
  # data
  for(i in 1:N){
    logLambda[i,1:M] ~ dmnorm(Mu[1:M], invSigma[1:M,1:M])
    for(j in 1:M){
      lambda[i,j] <- exp(logLambda[i,j])*S[i,j]
      Y[i,j] ~ dpois(lambda[i,j])
    }
  }
  # priors 
  invSigma[1:M,1:M] ~ dwish(invSigma0[1:M,1:M], nu0)
  for(j in 1:M){
    Mu[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.000001)
  }
  #
  Sigma[1:M,1:M] <- inverse(invSigma[,])
}
R2WinBUGS::write.model(wb.model, model.file) # write model file

# set data and initial values #
dat <- list(N=N,
            M=M,
            Y=Y, 
            S=S, 
            invSigma0=diag(M)/1000,
            nu0=M)
inits <- function(){
  logLambda <- log(Y/S+.1)
  list(
    logLambda = logLambda + rnorm(1,0,1),
    invSigma = solve(var(logLambda + rnorm(1,0,1))), 
    Mu = colMeans(logLambda) + rnorm(1,0,1)
  )
}

# run warm-up # 
jags <- jags.model(model.file,
                   data = dat, 
                   inits=inits, 
                   n.chains = 4,
                   n.adapt = 10000)

# update #
parameters <- c("Mu", "Sigma")
samples_jags <- samples <- coda.samples(jags,
                                        parameters,
                                        10000)

# summary # 
summary(samples)

It seems to work quite well. With Stan (code below), the posterior simulations seem to be in agreement with those generated by JAGS, but  I am facing two problems :

 1) I always get the warning :
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::wishart_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): WW is not positive definite (1.1694101865913203e+25:0).
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I'd like to know more about this warning. What should I do ? I don't think the model is ill-conditioned (BTW what does it mean?) nor misspecified.

 2) The sampling is extremely slow as compared to JAGS. Is it due to 1) ? 

Thanks for your attention. 

###########################
###     STAN model      ###
###########################
library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast") 

# write model #
model_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of individuals
  int<lower=0> M; // number of variables
  int<lower=0> Y[N, M];
  int<lower = 0> nu0;
  cov_matrix[M] Sigma0;
  real S[N,M];
}
parameters {
  cov_matrix[M] Sigma;
  vector[M] Mu; 
  vector[M] logLambda[N];
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[M] Lambda[N];
  for(i in 1:N){
    for(j in 1:M){
      Lambda[i,j] <- S[i,j]*exp(logLambda[i,j]);
    }
  }
}
model {
  for(i in 1:N){
    logLambda[i] ~ multi_normal(Mu, Sigma);
  }
  for(i in 1:N){
    Y[i] ~ poisson(Lambda[i]);
  }
  Sigma ~ wishart(nu0, Sigma0);
  Mu ~ normal(0, 1000);
}
"

# set data and initial values # 
dat <- list(N=N,
            M=M,
            Y=Y, 
            S=S, 
            Sigma0=diag(M)*1000,
            nu0=M)
inits <- function(){
  logLambda <- log(Y/S+.1)
  list(
    logLambda = logLambda + rnorm(1,0,1),
    Sigma = var(logLambda + rnorm(1,0,1)), 
    Mu = colMeans(logLambda) + rnorm(1,0,1)
  )
}

# compile model # 
model <- stan_model(model_code = model_code, model_name="tunaru")

# sample #
samples_stan <- samples <- sampling(model,  data = dat, init=inits, 
         iter = 20000, warmup=10000, chains = 4)

# summary # 
fit_ss <- extract(samples,  pars=c("Mu", "Sigma"), permuted=FALSE)
monitor(fit_ss, digits=2, warmup=0) # warmup is already removed by the extract() function

messages.author: 54e08ddecb38c1b3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
Hi Stéphane,

The warning is quite explicit: the matrix failed the positive definite test by a really really small number. This is a pretty common problem with priors on multivariate distribution.

A good exercise in frustration with this problem is to try to sample from a multivariate distribution with the package MASS in R with what you believe to be a positive-definite symmetric covariance matrix. Most often than not the matrix is not exactly positive-definite and you will have to thinker with it with and use a function like make.positive.definite() from the package corpcor to coerce the function to work.

As stated in the message itself this is not a serious problem unless you see the message really frequently. The message will invariably appear a few time right after you initialized the model, it will probably pop up randomly during the adaptation phase. It should have disappeared completely by the time you reach the sampling stage.  

As far as your second question is concerned all models will be slower in stan compared to jags. I believe this is even more apparent for multivariate models. I'm pretty sure the manual had a section on this part at some point although I haven't read the newer versions.  

However, and this is really important, for simple models stan will converge more quickly and will produce a higher number of effective sample sizes. As far as my experience with more complex models the advantage of stan over jags is that the model will ultimately converge... something I never achieved with jags.

Chris
------------

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
As Chris noted, you have to be careful with your comparisons.  Is the time per sample much larger,
or the time per _effective_ sample?  Only the latter matters for efficient inference.

If you are seeing larger times per effective sample then you may be running into issues with the 
Wishart prior.  Outside of conjugate models Wishart priors are notorious for inducing heavy tailed
posteriors which become difficult to fit.  Be aware that WinBUGS and JAGS aren’t necessarily
fitting them correctly, either, the Gibbs samplers they use are just less expressive to such
pathologies.

Thank you Chris & Michael. Your answers are really helpful.
 
About the slowness, I mean the total time, obtained by system.time(sampling(......)). 

I have chosen to try a model with a covariance matrix because I have seen that Stan allows prior distributions other than the Wishart distribution. I'd like to compare the different priors.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts: About the slowness, I mean the total time, obtained by system.time(sampling(......)).

Yeah, that’s not particularly helpful here.  HMC iterations take longer but yield MUCH
higher effective sample sizes and hence more efficient MCMC.
I have chosen to try a model with a covariance matrix because I have seen that Stan allows prior distributions other than the Wishart distribution. I'd like to compare the different priors.
Absolutely, that’s one of the great use cases for Stan and the LKJ priors are awesome.
Actually I used this model on real data when I was a WinBUGS user, and I remember the convergence was not clearly achieved.

It can be even more insidious than that as the chains might appear to have converged but still
be highly biased due to ergodicity issues.  I’d recommend at least confirming that your model
gets the right answers with simulated data.

Good luck.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
For (1), those are informational messages you can ignore if they
don't happen very often. You often see them in warmup until adaptation
has converged to a decent step size. It just indicates a Metropolis
rejection. The source is typically arithmetic issues with too large
step sizes in the discretization of the simulation of the Hamiltonian
dynamics in the HMC algorithm.

We're going to remove the message because it's been confusing our users.
We haven't been able to stress its informational nature enough to
stop worrying people.

For (2), are you sure you're getting the same answers from JAGS and Stan,
especially in terms of posterior variance?

If I'm remembering JAGS correctly, I don't think the JAGS and Stan
are identitcal. Stan uses covariance as its parameterization of
multi_normal, whereas I think JAGS uses precision matrices. So you
either want to use Stan's multi_normal_prec() or use the inverse Wishart
with appropriate priors. You can also make it even faster by
Cholesky factoring the covariance matrix outside of the loop
and using multi_normal_cholesky() within the loop instead of plain multi_normal().
See page 96 of the 2.2.0 manual.

Having said that, we have alternative recommendations
for priors at the end of the regression chapter that we think make more sense.
You can't code them in JAGS/BUGS because they're not conjugate, but they let
you shrink toward identity correlation (or take a uniform distribution on correlation)
and then have independently scales by dimension.

Stan can also be much more efficient at exploring fat tails and also at uncovering
what's effectively non-identifiability in the model. See the new manual
chapter on problematic posteriors.

Also for (2), are you measuring effective samples per second rather than just
iteration speed? Only the number of effective samples matters for inferences.
Often Stan has slower iterations, but better mixing.

We wouldn't recommend a normal(0,1000) prior unless you really expect your
Mu to be that huge. Again, see the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
for more info.

Finally, how are you initializing in both systems and what does the
number of iterations to convergence look like?

- Bob

>

Most often than not the matrix is not exactly positive-definite and you will have to thinker with it with and use a function like make.positive.definite() from the package corpcor to coerce the function to work.
>

>
> As far as your second question is concerned all models will be slower in stan compared to jags. I believe this is even more apparent for multivariate models. I'm pretty sure the manual had a section on this part at some point although I haven't read the newer versions.

I just want to clarify this one. It's not always the case that
Stan will be slower per iteration. There are some calculations where
doing all the conditionals winds up being very expensive.

> However, and this is really important, for simple models stan will converge more quickly and will produce a higher number of effective sample sizes. As far as my experience with more complex models the advantage of stan over jags is that the model will ultimately converge... something I never achieved with jags.
>

That was what motivated Andrew to hire us to build Stan in the first place :-)

And the ability to do some models that you can't express in JAGS. You'll
find JAGS and BUGS only let you do conjugate models for multivariate models.
In those cases, they're definitely faster if you code a direct translation into
Stan.

Sometimes you can exploit the conjugacy in Stan directly (there's a simple
example with beta-binomial samplers in the optimization chapter of the manual).
In other cases, if you can marginalize out a parameter, you can express the reduced
model in Stan. In fact, the latter is what we have to do for discrete parameters,
but you can also use the same strategy in some continuous cases.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
To be pedantic, it's an attempt at a flat prior and is at once not a great approximation (mathematically)
and too good of an approximation (practically).

The problem is that priors like this place a tremendous amount of probability mass at events way out
in the tails.  With little data your chains would spend most of their time around 1000, and if you seed
everything at O(1) the sampler will take forever to get out that far.  When you do have data but
your posterior is nasty and nonlinear the prior won't do anything, and you won't get any helpful
regularization.

But you have to deal with that, because if you set your prior to N(0, 1000) you're saying that 1000 is a 
perfectly reasonable value (that's what Bob meant when he said "expect Mu to be huge").  If you consider
values that large to be extreme then your prior shouldn't be N(0, 1000).  If 1000 isn't that extreme then
you probably want to rescale your system so that expected values are O(1).

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
There are two issues.  

Firstly there's the computational issue of floating point arithmetic.  Manipulating numbers all of the same order
is much more stable and accurate then numbers of wildly varying scales.  The adaptation algorithm also
assumes that the typical set is near parameter values around 1, and if the typical set is actually way off at 1000
then it will take forever to reach and the chains will converge only slowly.

Then there's the modeling issue.  Flat priors are counter-intuitive (flat is not non-informative in R^n) and allow 
likelihood pathologies (heavy-tails, extreme nonlinearities, etc) to propagate to the posterior.  Proper modeling requires 
identifying the relevant scales and encoding them in our prior.  

So if mu = 1000 is meaningful then go ahead and use it (although you really should rescale your problem to avoid 
the computation issues noted above).  But it's just some arbitrary "big number" you should spend some more time
modeling your problem.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts: Sorry but I don't know what is a typical set.

The typical set is the soft neighborhood containing the majority of the posterior probability mass
(the neighborhood becomes more concentrated and more sharply-defined as the dimensionality
of the posterior increases).  In other words, it's where the chain will spend all of its time.
And why does the algorithm assume something near 1 ?
Because most models in practice are built around such a scale.
By "scaling my problem", do you mean scaling the data ?

Standardizing your data might help, or you could explicitly define your posterior
with terms like 1000 * mu, mu ~ N(0, 1) instead of mu ~ N(0, 1000).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts: I'm currently having a very vague and naive idea of what Stan does : it writes down the posterior distribution and simulate a sample with an algorithm mainly requiring the posterior density and its derivatives. That's why I don't know why there is a difference between 1000 * mu, mu ~ N(0, 1)  and  mu ~ N(0, 1000).  Where does this difference occurs in the algorithm ?

Stan samples from a given posterior, but an ill-conditioned posterior will lead to inefficient sampling.  For example, a model with many varying scales,

x1 ~ normal(0, 1);
x2 ~ normal(0, 1000);

will be difficult to sample from.  This often happens implicitly in complicated likelihoods, but restricting the prior to reasonable values prevents
an ill-conditioned likelihood from producing an ill-conditioned posterior; i's the same principle as regularization.  If you are not familiar with
these ideas I recommend you check out any decent book on MCMC -- http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/book/ and http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/arm/
provide thorough discussions.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
The third edition of BDA covers HMC and the principles are ARM are extremely relevant when one understands the possible pathologies of HMC.

Now floating point arithmetic has a limited bandwidth.  In one dimension N(0, 1000) sacrifices dynamic range for resolution where as 1000 * N(0, 1) provides better dynamic range at lower resolution.  In practice the resolution is
negligible compared to Monte Carlo errors and posterior variance, so 1000 * N(0, 1) is preferable, especially when your posterior is diffuse.  Additionally, 1000 * N(0, 1), makes it easier to define good default starting points
and integrator step sizes when initializing the algorithms.

What's most important, however, is the multivariate case where you have N(0, 1000) and N(0, 1).  Transforming to 1000 * N(0, 1) and N(0, 1) ensures that both parameters are O(1), there is approximate rotation invariance and
consequently the numerical integrator becomes significantly more accurate.  More accuracy means higher performance.

But these are all very specific to HMC or our implementation of it.  The bigger deal is that N(0, 1000) is a diffuse prior and diffuse priors are annoying to sample from (the extreme being an unbounded uniform distribution which
will never converge in more than 2 dimensions).  When your likelihood is not particularly informative the posterior defaults to this diffusive behavior, which is why we are careful to recommend relatively informative priors for
robust inference

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow sampling and "WW is not positive definite" in wishart_log
parts:
Consider a three-dimensional model with parameters x, y, z.
Let the priors for each be N(0, 1000) but the likelihood only constrains y, z with N(0, 1).
Then the posterior is still N(0, 1000) in the x direction.

The point is that the likelihood is often uninformative on some subset of the parameters
(or, even worse, some nonlinear combination of the parameters).  Good choices of prior
distributions consistent with actual prior expectations helps to regularize such likelihoods.
